--- title: "The Lower Core PCE Path Is a New Ruler" pagetitle: "September 2026 BEA: core PCE 3.0%, Q2 GDP revised to 2.2%" date: "2026-10-10" author: Yoram Gilboa categories: [economics, inflation, federal reserve, data visualization] description: "Core PCE is 3.0 percent on the year after a measurement revision. July core moved from 3.3 to 3.0 percent. Q2 GDP was revised up from 1.5 to 2.2 percent." image: images/pce-yoy.png image-alt: "Headline and core PCE inflation over the year through August 26, with a 2 percent reference line" toc: true toc-location: right code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" title-block-banner: true body-classes: compact-charts css: ../../../styles.css format: html: title-prefix: "" --- The lower core PCE path is a new ruler on the same economy. On 9/30/26 the Bureau of Economic Analysis published the August 26 personal income report and the third estimate of second-quarter GDP, and with them this year's annual update. The update changed three price methods and applied the new methods back to January 2021. A vintage is the version of that history published as of one date. The date is the evaluation date of the dataset. It fixes which official record you are reading, and a later BEA release is a new evaluation of the same months. Every figure below is the vintage as of 9/30/26. BEA described the three changes in its [preview of this year's annual update](https://apps.bea.gov/scb/issues/2026/06-june/0626-nea-preview.htm). Portfolio management and investment advice services no longer take their price from the producer price index for that industry. BEA now estimates the quantity with a Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll series, and the price is what remains after that quantity is removed from nominal spending. Legal services no longer use the consumer price index. That index was last published for September 2024, and the unpublished values BEA had been using did not meet Bureau of Labor Statistics quality guidelines. The replacement, beginning in 2024, is a composite of producer price indexes for household legal services. Computer software and accessories no longer use the consumer price index alone. The replacement blends that index with producer price indexes for game software and for information-technology infrastructure. [RBC Economics](https://www.rbc.com/en/economics/us-analysis/us-featured-analysis/pce-deflator-update-a-retroactive-revision-not-a-disinflationary-signal/) put magnitudes on that preview before the release. The three changes together were expected to lower the annual core rate by 18 basis points, taking July 26 core from 3\.3% to 3\.1%. Portfolio management was the small slice. RBC had the old deflator averaging 14\.1% over the year since December 2023, and the implied new index averaging 12\.3%. At a weight of 1\.7% of core, that difference was about 3 basis points of the core rate. In this file, July 26 core then moved from 3\.30% to 2\.98%, a gap of 32 basis points. That gap is larger than the whole preview. BEA does not assign it to portfolio management. Morning coverage led with the headline revisions. [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-second-quarter-gdp-revised-higher-amid-robust-consumer-spending-2026-09-30/) reported second-quarter real GDP of 2\.2%, revised up 0\.7 percentage point from 1\.5%, alongside the new inflation rates. The PCE price index measures the prices people pay for goods and services, including purchases made on their behalf. Core PCE is that index without food and energy. In August 26, core PCE is 3\.0% over the year and rose 0\.2% on the month. Headline PCE rose 0\.3% on the month and 3\.4% over the year. The year rate moved because earlier months were remeasured. On the prior release, core inflation in July 26 was **3\.3%** over the year. On this vintage it is **3\.0%**. Headline inflation for that month is 3\.4%, compared with 3\.7% before. That gap is a level shift in the rewritten history. The August 26 month change is the new price observation, and the three-month core pace on this vintage is 2\.0%. BEA's news release does not split that core revision into a methodology share and a source-data share. A same-day [account of fed-funds futures](https://www.investmentnews.com/equities/pce-data-cools-but-further-rate-hikes-loom/268415) marked down a hike at the 10/28/26 meeting and left a later meeting this year as the more likely date of the next increase. Those odds are not in this snapshot. The same preview said the regional accounts would begin their annual update that day for the first time. The national update and the GDP third estimate were published together. The release also closed the setup this blog left open on 9/26/26. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Reproducing this analysis The figures below are drawn from the committed snapshot for the 9/30/26 release. To rebuild them from this folder, run `scripts/01_fetch_data.py`, then `scripts/02_clean_data.py`, then `scripts/04_compute_stats.py`. The first script checks the saved FRED files and does not download a new vintage. Monthly history runs through August 26. The July 26 rates from the earlier release, and the second-estimate columns in the GDP chart, are copied from the BEA pages linked in the notes. Data come from the [Bureau of Economic Analysis](https://www.bea.gov/) by way of [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Note on data The charts use the committed FRED snapshot in this folder. Rebuilding checks that snapshot and does not download a later vintage. Current FRED does not keep the pre-update path. The previously published year rates for July 26, the earlier real-spending print, and the earlier saving rate are copied from the personal-income release for that month. Second-estimate GDP, private domestic final sales, and real gross domestic income are copied from the third-estimate comparison table. Food, energy, and core month changes are each index's own change. They do not add up to the headline change. The quarterly PCE price rates in the growth section are annualized quarter-to-quarter rates. They are a different statistic from the monthly year rates. BEA's news release does not assign a basis-point share of the core revision to the three price methods. The method descriptions are the Bureau's preview, not a contribution table. The RBC basis points, the old portfolio deflator, and the implied new index are transcribed from that pre-release note. They are not BEA prints. The July core gap in basis points is the prior one-decimal rate minus the updated hundredths in this file. The August 26 saving rate and the saving rate published for July 26 before this release are different vintages. ::: ::: {#31458a0c .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Inflation over the past year Each line is the percent change from the same month a year earlier. Headline is the full price index. Core is that index without food and energy. At the right edge, in August 26, headline is 3\.4% and core is 3\.0%. Both lines are only the vintage as of 9/30/26. They do not draw the path as it stood before the annual update. The table is the level shift. July 26 has two evaluation dates. The earlier release was published to one decimal. The other columns keep the hundredths, so July 26 now and August 26 are not the same figure. They still match when rounded to one decimal. The first two columns are the rewrite of one month. The third column is the new month on the new ruler. | | July 26 earlier | July 26 now | August 26 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Headline | 3\.70% | 3\.36% | 3\.42% | | Core | 3\.30% | 2\.98% | 3\.01% | The dashed line is the Fed's 2% aim. Both year rates are still above it. The chart ends in August 26. ::: {#cell-fig-pce-yoy .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The year rates are already in the cleaned monthly file. This cell draws them. yoy = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "pce_monthly.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True) yoy = monthly_calendar(yoy, "2023-01-01", "2026-08-01", ["pce_price_yoy", "core_price_yoy"]) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6)) ax.plot(yoy.index, yoy["pce_price_yoy"], color=COLORS["primary"], linewidth=1.8, zorder=3) ax.plot(yoy.index, yoy["core_price_yoy"], color=COLORS["secondary"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=3) ax.axhline( stats["fed_target"], color=COLORS["fed_target"], linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.8, zorder=2, ) ax.text( yoy.index[2], stats["fed_target"] + 0.15, f"Fed {fmt(stats['fed_target'])}% aim", color=COLORS["fed_target"], fontsize=8, alpha=0.8, ) last_x = yoy.index[-1] ax.scatter( [last_x, last_x], [yoy["pce_price_yoy"].iloc[-1], yoy["core_price_yoy"].iloc[-1]], s=40, color=[COLORS["primary"], COLORS["secondary"]], zorder=5, edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, ) span = last_x - yoy.index[0] ax.set_xlim(yoy.index[0] - span * 0.02, last_x + span * 0.14) label_endpoints( ax, [ { "x": last_x, "y": yoy["pce_price_yoy"].iloc[-1], "text": f"Headline {yoy['pce_price_yoy'].iloc[-1]:.1f}%", "color": COLORS["primary"], }, { "x": last_x, "y": yoy["core_price_yoy"].iloc[-1], "text": f"Core {yoy['core_price_yoy'].iloc[-1]:.1f}%", "color": COLORS["secondary"], }, ], ) ax.set_ylabel("Percent change from a year earlier") year_ticks(ax, yoy.index) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "pce-yoy.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Percent change from a year earlier for headline and core PCE.](index_files/figure-html/fig-pce-yoy-output-1.png){#fig-pce-yoy width=789 height=449} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: [BEA Personal Income and Outlays](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-august-2026), price indexes via [FRED headline PCE](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPI) and [FRED core PCE](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPILFE). Prior rates from the [previous personal-income release](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026). ::: A year rate looks back twelve months, so the annual update can move it by rewriting earlier months. The step from July 26 to August 26 on this vintage is small next to the rewrite of July 26 itself. The next chart is the price change in August 26 by itself. ## What changed in August A month percent change compares this month's price index with last month's. Headline prices in August 26 rose 0\.3%, and core prices rose 0\.2%. On the updated vintage, the July 26 month rates are 0\.1% for headline and 0\.1% for core. A year rate compares a month with the same month a year earlier. That is the division in the table above. From July 26 to August 26, the new month enters that twelve-month window and August 2025 drops out. The year rate changes by the new month's price change minus the price change in the month that drops out. For headline prices, August 26 rose 0\.31% and August 2025 rose 0\.25%, so the year rate moves by 0\.06 percentage point, from 3\.36% to 3\.42%. Core is calculated the same way. In the table its year rate goes from 2\.98% to 3\.01%. That arithmetic stays on one vintage. It is separate from the level shift between the first two columns. Food prices were 0\.0% on the month. Energy goods and services prices rose 2\.3%. Those two series are chain-type price indexes of their own. Adding them to core does not recover the headline 0\.3%, and the chart does not stack them. Within August 26, energy is the large bar. Core's 0\.2% is the new month's underlying print. It is separate from the year-rate rewrite in the chart above. The bars run for the twelve months ending August 26. Across those months, energy prices range from \-5\.8% in June 26 to 11\.5% in March 26. The 2\.3% increase in August 26 is the latest reading in that range. ::: {#cell-fig-pce-monthly .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The month changes are already in the cleaned price file. This cell draws them. prices = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "pce_price_monthly.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True) prices = monthly_calendar( prices, "2025-09-01", "2026-08-01", ["food_price_mom", "energy_price_mom", "core_price_mom"], ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2)) x = np.arange(len(prices)) width = 0.26 ax.bar(x - width, prices["food_price_mom"], width, color=COLORS["warning"], edgecolor="white", label="Food") ax.bar(x, prices["energy_price_mom"], width, color=COLORS["accent"], edgecolor="white", label="Energy") ax.bar(x + width, prices["core_price_mom"], width, color=COLORS["primary"], edgecolor="white", label="Core") ax.axhline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8) ax.set_xticks(x) ax.set_xticklabels( [ short_year(d.strftime("%b\n%Y") if d.month in (1, 9) else d.strftime("%b")) for d in prices.index ] ) ax.set_ylabel("Percent change from the prior month") ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left") plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "pce-monthly.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Monthly price changes for food, energy, and core PCE. Each bar is that index's own change, and the three do not add up to headline inflation.](index_files/figure-html/fig-pce-monthly-output-1.png){#fig-pce-monthly width=789 height=408} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: [BEA Table 2.8.4 price indexes](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-august-2026), via [FRED food prices](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFXARG3M086SBEA), [FRED energy prices](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DNRGRG3M086SBEA), and [FRED core PCE](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPILFE). ::: Inside August 26, the inflation news is a modest core month plus a jump in energy prices. The lower year rate is the rewritten history. Spending is a separate cut of the same release. ## Spending and income Nominal spending is the cash-register total. Real spending removes the price change, so it is closer to the quantity households bought. Disposable personal income is income after personal current taxes. Real disposable income removes the price change from that after-tax income. The dollar changes below are changes in seasonally adjusted annual-rate levels. They are not the dollars households spent or received during August 26 alone. The real PCE dollar change is in chained 2017 dollars. The percent changes are monthly rates. In August 26, current-dollar PCE rose 0\.9%. That is the cash-register percent change. Real PCE, the quantity, rose 0\.6%, from 0\.1% in revised July 26. Personal income rose 0\.2%, or $66\.6 billion at an annual rate. Current-dollar disposable income rose 0\.3%, or $68\.6 billion at an annual rate, and real disposable income was 0\.0%. Households spent more in real terms in a month when real after-tax income did not rise. In annual-rate dollars, current-dollar PCE rose $190\.8 billion, with goods up $114\.1 billion and services up $76\.7 billion. Real PCE rose $92\.8 billion in chained 2017 dollars. The lines below index both real series to January 2024 = 100, so the paths can share a scale. By August 26 the spending index is 107\.7 and the after-tax income index is 104\.1. The saving rate, personal saving as a share of disposable income, is not on the chart. On this vintage it was 4\.1% in August 26 and 4\.6% in July 26. The 3\.0% figure is the July 26 rate published before the annual update. Putting 4\.1% next to that older 3\.0% mixes a new month with the old ruler. On the new vintage the saving rate is lower in August 26 than in July 26. ::: {#cell-fig-real-spending-income .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The index is already in the cleaned file. The base month equals 100. real = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "real_indexes.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True) real = monthly_calendar(real, "2024-01-01", "2026-08-01", ["real_pce_index", "real_dpi_index"]) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6)) ax.plot(real.index, real["real_pce_index"], color=COLORS["primary"], linewidth=1.8, zorder=3) ax.plot(real.index, real["real_dpi_index"], color=COLORS["secondary"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=3) last_x = real.index[-1] ax.scatter( [last_x, last_x], [real["real_pce_index"].iloc[-1], real["real_dpi_index"].iloc[-1]], s=40, color=[COLORS["primary"], COLORS["secondary"]], zorder=5, edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, ) span = last_x - real.index[0] ax.set_xlim(real.index[0] - span * 0.02, last_x + span * 0.16) label_endpoints( ax, [ { "x": last_x, "y": real["real_pce_index"].iloc[-1], "text": f"Real PCE {real['real_pce_index'].iloc[-1]:.1f}", "color": COLORS["primary"], }, { "x": last_x, "y": real["real_dpi_index"].iloc[-1], "text": f"Real income {real['real_dpi_index'].iloc[-1]:.1f}", "color": COLORS["secondary"], }, ], ) ax.set_ylabel(f"Index, {stats['index_base']} = 100") half_year_ticks(ax, real.index) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "real-spending-income.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Real spending and real after-tax income on one index, with the latest month's percent changes stated in the text above.](index_files/figure-html/fig-real-spending-income-output-1.png){#fig-real-spending-income width=783 height=448} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: [BEA Personal Income and Outlays](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-august-2026), via [FRED real PCE](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEC96) and [FRED real disposable income](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DSPIC96). ::: Real spending rose in a month when real after-tax income did not. The quarterly estimates were revised up, and BEA's notes name where that extra growth came from. ## The second-quarter revision The chart compares the second and third estimates for real GDP, private domestic final sales, and real gross domestic income. Those are the aggregate growth rates in BEA's comparison table. Real GDP was revised from 1\.5% to 2\.2%. The advance estimate had also been 1\.5%. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, household consumption plus private fixed investment, went from 4\.2% to 4\.6%. The advance reading of that measure was 3\.9%. Real gross domestic income, the income-side twin of GDP, went from 2\.2% to 2\.6%. BEA attributes that 0\.7 percentage point primarily to investment, consumer spending, and government spending. Investment includes both inventories and fixed investment. ::: {.callout-note} ## Data centers in the structures revision Nonresidential structures led the fixed-investment revision. BEA names commercial and health care construction, mainly data centers, from revised Census construction data for May and June. That is the data-center buildout inside this GDP table. It is a revision to construction put in place. Energy prices are the other reading of that buildout in this post: energy goods and services rose 2\.3% in August 26. One line is building spending. The other is a price index. ::: Outside that structures line, residential investment was led by improvements, on revised remodeler payrolls. Consumer services were led by recreation, including spectator amusements, and by social and religious services, partly offset by lower air transportation. Goods were led by recreational goods and vehicles, including information processing equipment. The government piece was mainly federal defense. BEA ties that defense revision to updated seasonal adjustment factors, so it is a statistical artifact in the seasonal pattern rather than a new round of spending. Two price rates in that same table are easy to mix up with the monthly path. The quarterly PCE price index rose at a 5\.0% annual rate, revised down 0\.3 percentage point from 5\.3%. Core was 3\.3%, revised down the same 0\.3 percentage point from 3\.6%. Those are quarter-to-quarter annualized rates for the spring quarter. The August 26 year rates are 3\.4% and 3\.0%. First-quarter real GDP is now 2\.5%, an upward revision of 0\.4 percentage point, primarily from services exports and from consumer spending on goods and services. The GDP update covers the first quarter of 2021 through the first quarter of 26. The reference year remains 2017. ::: {#cell-fig-q2-revision .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Second-estimate values are copied from the BEA comparison table. # Third-estimate GDP and private final sales are the latest FRED vintage. revision = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "q2_revision.csv") order = revision.iloc[::-1].reset_index(drop=True) y = np.arange(len(order)) height = 0.36 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2)) ax.barh( y + height / 2, order["second"], height=height, color=COLORS["light"], edgecolor="white", label="Second estimate", ) ax.barh( y - height / 2, order["third"], height=height, color=COLORS["primary"], edgecolor="white", label="Third estimate", ) for i, row in order.iterrows(): ax.text(row["second"] + 0.08, i + height / 2, f"{row['second']:.1f}", fontsize=8, color=COLORS["neutral"], va="center") ax.text(row["third"] + 0.08, i - height / 2, f"{row['third']:.1f}", fontsize=8, color=COLORS["neutral"], va="center") ax.set_yticks(y) ax.set_yticklabels(order["measure"]) ax.set_xlabel("Percent change, seasonally adjusted annual rate") ax.set_xlim(0, max(order["second"].max(), order["third"].max()) + 1.2) ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right") plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "q2-revision.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Second-estimate and third-estimate growth rates for real GDP, private domestic final sales, and real gross domestic income.](index_files/figure-html/fig-q2-revision-output-1.png){#fig-q2-revision width=789 height=408} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: [BEA GDP third estimate](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/gdp-third-estimate-industries-corporate-profits-state-gdp-and-state-personal-income-2nd). Latest GDP and private final sales also via [FRED real GDP](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A191RL1Q225SBEA) and [FRED private domestic final purchases](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PB0000031Q225SBEA). ::: Growth was revised up. The lower year rate is the new price ruler. Whether 3\.0% is also the recent pace is a different cut of the same price index. ## The recent pace The year rate is the change over twelve months. The three-month pace compounds only the latest three months, as if that stretch had lasted a year. On the 9/30/26 vintage, core's three-month pace is 2\.0% and the twelve-month rate is 3\.0%. Both lines use that vintage. The sample ends in August 26. ::: {#cell-fig-core-pace .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The twelve-month rate and the three-month pace are already in the cleaned file. pace = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "core_pace.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True) pace = monthly_calendar(pace, "2023-01-01", "2026-08-01", ["core_price_yoy", "core_3m"]) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6)) ax.plot(pace.index, pace["core_price_yoy"], color=COLORS["primary"], linewidth=1.8, zorder=3) ax.plot(pace.index, pace["core_3m"], color=COLORS["warning"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=3) ax.axhline( stats["fed_target"], color=COLORS["fed_target"], linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.8, ) last_x = pace.index[-1] ax.scatter( [last_x, last_x], [pace["core_price_yoy"].iloc[-1], pace["core_3m"].iloc[-1]], s=40, color=[COLORS["primary"], COLORS["warning"]], zorder=5, edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, ) span = last_x - pace.index[0] ax.set_xlim(pace.index[0] - span * 0.02, last_x + span * 0.18) y_12 = float(pace["core_price_yoy"].iloc[-1]) y_3m = float(pace["core_3m"].iloc[-1]) label_endpoints( ax, [ { "x": last_x, "y": y_12, "text": f"12-month {y_12:.1f}%", "color": COLORS["primary"], }, ], ) # The three-month pace ends on the aim line, so its label sits above the point. label_y = y_3m + 0.35 ax.plot( [last_x, last_x], [y_3m, label_y], color=COLORS["light"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=4, ) ax.text( last_x, label_y, f" 3-month {y_3m:.1f}%", fontsize=8, color=COLORS["warning"], va="center", fontweight="bold", ) ax.set_ylabel("Percent") year_ticks(ax, pace.index) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(IMG_DIR / "core-pace.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Core PCE over the past year and the compounded three-month pace, both on the updated vintage.](index_files/figure-html/fig-core-pace-output-1.png){#fig-core-pace width=789 height=449} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: [BEA core PCE price index](https://www.bea.gov/data/personal-consumption-expenditures-price-index-excluding-food-and-energy), via [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPILFE). ::: The three-month pace sits on the 2% aim. The year rate is still 3\.0%. The short line is only the latest three months on the new ruler. It does not undo the rewritten months inside the twelve-month rate. ## Same months, new ruler The 9/26/26 post stopped before this print. The print is now in. Core PCE is 3\.0% over the year because the annual update remeasured the history back to January 2021. The July 26 core rate moved from 3\.3% to 3\.0% on that new ruler. August 26 core prices rose 0\.2% on the month, and the three-month pace is 2\.0%. Those two are the trend reads in this file. Second-quarter real GDP is 2\.2%, revised up from 1\.5%. Real spending rose 0\.6% in August 26. ### What it means for **For the Fed.** On 9/16/26 the Federal Reserve set the funds rate at 3\.75 to 4\.00 percent. The [September projections](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcprojtabl20260916.htm) put the median for the end of 26 at 4\.1%. 12 of 18 participants looked for exactly one more increase in 26. Those projections sit one quarter point above the current range's midpoint. They were submitted before 9/30/26, and they are participant projections, not a Committee vote. This release does not rewrite them. The futures account cited above marked down a hike at the 10/28/26 meeting and left a later meeting this year as the more likely date of the next increase. The odds themselves are not in this dataset, and neither is the decision at the next meeting. **For households.** The year rates, 3\.0% for core and 3\.4% for headline, compare August 26 with a year earlier on the new ruler. They are not a new claim that prices fell during August 26. Real after-tax income was unchanged that month, at 0\.0%. Real spending rose 0\.6%. **For investors.** The federal funds target range remains 3\.75 to 4\.00 percent. Policy rates influence borrowing costs and the rates investors use to discount future cash flows. This release lowers the published inflation path because the ruler changed. It does not, by itself, change the policy setting. ### What to watch - The September [consumer price index](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/2026/10_sched_list.htm) on 10/14/26. - The September [producer price index](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/2026/10_sched_list.htm) on 10/15/26. - The next [FOMC decision](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm) on 10/28/26. - [September PCE and the first look at third-quarter GDP](https://www.bea.gov/news/schedule) on 10/29/26. None of those prints is in this post. ## Limitations - The annual update is a level shift in measured prices. It is separate from the August 26 month change and from the three-month pace. - BEA names three new price methods and does not publish a basis-point split of the core revision between those methods and ordinary source-data updates. The basis points in the opening are RBC's preview and this file's July gap. They are not that missing BEA split. - The saving rate published for July 26 before the update and the August 26 saving rate are different vintages. The comparison inside the new vintage is revised July 26 against August 26. - Fed-funds futures are not in this snapshot. The post reports the direction described in same-day accounts and does not quote an odds figure. - Food, energy, and core month changes do not add up to the headline percent change. - The second-estimate bars exist because BEA printed the comparison. They are not a second FRED vintage stored beside the new one. - September prices and the October policy decision sit outside this file. ## Methodology | Series | What this post uses it for | Source |
